full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN. This overturns the first pass, which called it a variant.** I found a group that has studied this kind of model directly, and it reports this exact sequence.

**The near-exact match.** David Pinto-Ramos, Anudeep Surendran and Ricardo Martinez-Garcia have a preprint titled "Higher-Order Competition as a Minimal Mechanism for Spatial Pattern Diversity in Population Dynamics." Its code and data are on Zenodo (Pinto-Ramos, David. Surendran, Anudeep. Martinez-Garcia, Ricardo.), and Pinto-Ramos's site says it covers individual-based and PDE simulations, analysis scripts and figure material. Its showcase figure describes the same thing you observed: "Each dot represents an individual. As higher-order competition increases, the population reorganises into spots, stripes and gaps." The announcement also explains why your baseline is spots: "For a broad class of interaction kernels, pairwise competition produces only hexagonal arrays of population clusters." The authors say they show how higher-order competition enables stripes and gaps to emerge from competition alone. We analytically explain the restriction imposed by pairwise competition and derive the thresholds that govern the selection of different patterns. Your model has the same setup (only competition, a nonlocal pairwise kernel plus a three-body crowding term, continuous-space births and deaths) and the same control parameter.

**The spots coming back at higher death/birth ratio is also documented.** In vegetation and nonlocal-logistic models, raising mortality gives the standard order gaps → labyrinths/stripes → spots. A recent nonlocal model reports that as Da⁻ increases, representing worsening environmental conditions through a higher mortality rate, the model shows a sequence of gaps, labyrinths, and spots. The Lefever–Lejeune line of work describes a general sequence from patterns where the minima of the vegetation density form a lattice possessing a hexagonal symmetry, to stripes … succeeded then, by patterns where the maxima of the vegetation density are distributed as to form a hexagonal lattice. One review calls gaps, labyrinths and spots the standard sequence of patterns in vegetation models. So spots reappearing beyond the stripes at death/birth ≈ 0.55 is the standard spots → stripes → gaps diagram run in reverse. It is not a new twist.

**Real pattern or artifact?** These look like real emergent patterns. The ordered sequence and the anisotropy jump at the stripe transition match the documented pattern-selection thresholds; a random colouring or a frozen state would not give that. Two caveats about the measurements:
- The "hexagonal spots" g (3.27e-6) is just the bottom of the sweep, so it is the pairwise baseline, not a transition point.
- An anisotropy index jumping exactly from 0 to 1.0 suggests a saturating, near-binary measure, so it is not a precise order parameter.

**Searches run:** nonlocal competition spots/stripes/gaps in individual-based models; the Lefever–Lejeune spots/labyrinths/gaps sequence; the preprint title; the authors with "higher-order competition".

**What I couldn't check:** I only saw the authors' website, the Zenodo record, a LinkedIn announcement and search snippets, not the preprint itself. So I can't confirm that the spots coming back against death/birth ratio is shown inside that paper specifically, though it is standard in the related literature. I also didn't confirm the first pass's Britton citations.
